Abstract. The “up3bd” code, which is an efficient three-dimensional (3D) electrostatic parti-
cle-in-cell (PIC) simulation code for study of transport dynamics in fusion boundary layer 
plasmas or other plasmas in nature, has been tested on various high-performance computing 
(HPC) systems which consist of different types of processor. The results of benchmark tests 
indicate that the up3bd code works faster on processors in which cache memory is larger or 
memory bandwidth is broader. Also, the types of computations that each architecture excels 
at and struggles with has been revealed. 
Keywords: particle-in-cell, boundary layer plasma, high-performance computing 
1. Introduction 
Plasma particle simulation with the particle-in-cell (PIC) method [1] is a powerful tool 
for investigation of microscopic dynamics in various plasma phenomena. However, since the 
motions of many particles should be computed in such a particle simulation, it needs huge 
computer resources which have many processors and large memories. Using the PIC method, 
we have developed an efficient three-dimensional (3D) electrostatic plasma particle simula-
tion code, named “up3bd”, in order to research kinetic behaviors of transport phenomena in 
fusion boundary layer plasmas or other plasmas in nature [2-4]. The up3bd code is an updated 
version of our previous code named “p3bd” [5]. Using the p3bd and up3bd codes, we have 
made significant progress in research of fusion boundary layer plasma transport [6-8]. In the

2. Outline of the up3bd code 
In this section, we briefly describe the outline of the up3bd code. The up3bd code is a 
three-dimensional electrostatic particle-in-cell simulation code in which a particle absorbing 
condition is applied in some directions. The calculation flow is as follows [2]. 
1. Subroutine “init”: Initial positions and velocities of all simulation plasma particles are 
provided, that is, “particle loading” is performed. 
2. Subroutine “charge”: Charge densities on all grids are computed from particle posi-
tions, that is, charges of particles are assigned to grids. 
3. Subroutine “field”: Applying a finite difference approximation to the Poisson’s equa-
tion, electric potentials on all grids are solved with the fast Fourier transform (FFT) through 
the three-dimensional FFT library, “PoissonFFT2” [2]. Electric fields on all grids are given 
by a difference of the electric potential. 
4. Subroutine “accel”: Accelerations of all particles, i.e., velocities at a next time step, 
are calculated by the equation of motion, i.e., the Newton-Lorentz equation. 
5. Subroutine “move”: Positions of all particles are developed with the velocities. 
6. Subroutine “pact”: Numbers of particles which are out of the system, i.e., have been 
absorbed, are stored. Also, numbers of particles moved to the next domains are kept in other 
arrays. In this process, each particle is initially assigned a flag indicating whether it is within 
the current domain, in a neighboring domain, or outside the system. Subsequently, a unique 
index is assigned to each particle among those sharing the same flag. 
7. Subroutine “adjust”: Data of non-active particles which are out of the system or do-

8. Subroutine “bsort”: Particle data are sorted by the in-place bucket sorting method, 
which is called once every several tens of time steps. 
9: Return to subroutine “charge” (No. 2). 
3. Outline of optimizations 
As mentioned in Sec.1, the domain decomposition method is adopted in the up3bd code. 
In the 2D domain decomposition case, the data transfer between domains, i.e., processes, is 
separated into vertical and horizontal directions because this way is faster than that with a 
single call to transfer subroutines [3]. In the data transfer procedure, particles which move out 
to the next domains should be found. This computation is performed in the subroutines “pacty” 
and “pactz” which are the subroutine “pact” in the y and z directions, respectively. In these 
subroutines, there are do-loops including recurrence formula type calculations, which take 
long computation times on scalar processors. Thus, some modifications have been applied in 
these subroutines for scalar processors, as shown in Ref. [3]. On the other hand, because the 
do-loops including recurrence formula type calculations can be vectorized, such calculations 
are carried out fast in vector processors without any modifications. 
On vector processors, a calculation of charge density which is computed in a subroutine 
“charge” requires the most computational cost. Therefore, a work array whose size is 256 
(vector length) times larger than the charge density array is prepared to make the computation 
faster as shown in Fig. 1. Here, the size of the charge density array is equal to the number of 
grids in a domain. This optimization increases the vector operation ratio to over 99%, com-
pared to approximately 50% in the original implementation. Consequently, the execution 
speed of the optimized subroutine “charge” is approximately four times higher than that of 
the original. However, this method is not effective in the case of hybrid parallelization, in 
which both distributed and shared (thread) parallelizations are adopted, because the size of 
the work array increases by a factor of the number of threads. In the hybrid case, the compu-
tation is vectorized with a list-vector instruction without a large work array.

the up3bd code, the subroutine “bsort” is implemented that uses an in-place bucket sorting 
method. The sorting is also effective in the case of flat-MPI (message passing interface) par-
allelization on vector processors. Sorting ensures that particles within the same cell have sim-
ilar indices, which improves cache locality and allows field data such as the electric field and

4. Benchmark tests 
4.1. Comparison of performance 
We have tested the up3bd code in which the fundamental optimizations shown in Sec. 3 
279


                Journal of Advanced Simulation in Science and Engineering 
6 
 
were applied on four HPC systems, the Plasma Simulator (Vector Engine (VE) Type 10AE, 
NEC SX-Aurora TSUBASA) at NIFS, FLOW Type I (A64FX, Fujitsu FX1000) at the Infor-
mation Technology Center, Nagoya University, Camphor3 (Intel Xeon CPU Max 9480, 
DELL PowerEdge C6620) at ACCMS, Kyoto University, and AOBA-B (AMD EPYC7702, 
NEC LX406Rz-2) at the Cyberscience Center, Tohoku University. In the benchmark compu-
tations, the system size is 64×64×256 cells, the average number of particles per cell is 144, 
and a periodic boundary condition is applied in the y and z directions. The elapsed time for 
the 100 time steps without an initial setting and data I/O has been measured in each computa-
tion. The results are listed in Table 2. Here, although the hybrid parallelization (4 MPI pro-
cesses and 12 threads) is applied to the computation on FLOW Type I, the flat-MPI parallel-
ization (32 MPI processes) is configured in the computations on the other systems. Further-
more, in an estimation of the effective performance ratio shown in Table 2, it is assumed that 
a number of floating-point operations is the same for all computations and the value for 
AOBA-B is set as 1.0. The result of preliminary benchmark tests shown in Table 2 indicates 
that AOBA-B (EPYC7702) seems to be most suitable for the up3bd code among the four 
systems. This fact is considered to arise from the differences in cache memory size and 
memory bandwidth, depending on the type of processor. In PIC simulations, field data around 
a particle position must be accessed to compute charge density and particle acceleration. Such 
access to field data occur for all particles and then are thought to be performed more effi-
ciently with larger cache memory or broader memory bandwidth. 
Table 3 shows the ratios between the elapsed time of each subroutine and the total 
elapsed time. From such a table, we can find a bottleneck computation. This table indicates 
that the bottleneck subroutines differ depending on the system, or more specifically, the ar-
chitecture. On vector machines, the subroutine “charge” incurs the highest computational cost 
because the addition into field data within the subroutine “charge” is typically random, mak-
ing vectorization difficult. On the other hand, in Camphor3, the subroutine “accel” requires 
the most time, which is thought to be due to the random access pattern of reading field data. 
If the cache memory is small, frequent access to field data becomes necessary. Meanwhile, in 
AOBA-B, the subroutines “pact” and “adjust” are time-consuming, likely due to the overhead 
associated with inter-process communication. In FLOW Type I, the subroutine field (FFT) is 
the most costly, but the reasons for this require further investigation.

4.2. Comparison of scaling 
Figures 2 and 3 show weak and strong scaling. From these figures, we find that the par-
allelization on Camphor3 is performed more efficiently. This fact, along with the observation 
in Table 3 of the previous subsection that the subroutines “pact” and “adjust” and the subrou-
tine “field” are executed quickly in Camphor3, suggests that inter-process communication in 
Camphor3 is faster compared to other systems. On the other hand, AOBA-B exhibits a sig-
nificant performance degradation when the number of MPI processes increases from 32 to 
128. This is likely because both computations are executed on a single node, causing the 
amount of cache memory and memory bandwidth per process to be reduced to one-fourth.

5. Summary and future works 
In this work, we have investigated the computation performance of the efficient 
three-dimensional electrostatic particle-in-cell simulation code called “up3bd” on various ar-
chitectures which are NEC Vector Engine Type 10AE, Fujitsu A64FX, Intel Xeon CPU Max 
9480, and AMD EPYC7702. The results indicate that the up3bd code works faster on pro-
cessors in which cache memory is larger or memory bandwidth is broader as shown in Sec. 
4.1. Furthermore, this study has revealed the types of computations that each architecture ex-
cels at and struggles with. This finding will provide valuable insights for the future develop-
ment of a code tailored to each architecture. 
In the benchmark tests performed in this work, the size of the simulation system was 
small. Thus, we will carry out huge-scale simulations on those HPC systems and analyze the 
performance of parallelization regarding each system. Also, advanced optimizations of the 
up3bd code for each type of processor will be considered in the near future. Furthermore, we 
will install Coulomb collisions and atomic processes [12] into the up3bd code in order to in-
vestigate non-diffusive transports in a detachment state [13] and develop a procedure which 
can set various configurations of magnetic field and boundary conditions in order to imple-
ment “realistic plasma particle simulations”.
